Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that pure water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of dye) enters the tank at a rate of $13\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (13\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (13\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

Note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume of solution in the tank remains $260\,\text{L}.$
Then, since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{260}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $13\,\text{L/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(13\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{260}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(13\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{260}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{13Q}{260}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{20}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{Q}{20} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{20}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{20} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{1}{20})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{1}{20}\int \,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{t}{20}+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-t/20+C} \\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-t/20},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{kg}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ A{e}^{-0/20} & =18 \\ A & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18{e}^{-t/20}
$$
